abstract: The Forecasting Research Institute (FRI), in collaboration with the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, Yale School of Management, Stanford University, and University of Pennsylvania, surveyed 69 leading economists, 52 AI industry and policy experts, 38 superforecasters, and 401 general public members from October 2025 to February 2026 on the expected economic effects of AI. Economists assign a 47% probability to moderate AI progress by 2030 (semi-autonomous labs, five-day coding tasks completed by AI) and 14% to rapid progress (AI outperforming humans at many tasks), for a combined 61% probability of at least moderate progress. Under a rapid progress scenario, economists forecast 3.5% annualized GDP growth by 2030 and labor force participation declining to 59.1% (from 62.6% baseline), with AI accounting for roughly 10 million fewer workers. By 2050 in the rapid scenario, median economists predict labor force participation at 55% and wealth concentration at 80% in the top 10% — a level last seen in 1939. A key tension emerges: economists expect significant AI capability improvements but anticipate economic indicators will remain close to historical trends, citing uneven adoption, multi-decade technology diffusion lags, and demographic headwinds.
keyFindings: Economists assign 61% probability to at least moderate AI progress by 2030, with 14% probability of rapid progress where AI outperforms humans at many tasks.

Under rapid AI progress, economists forecast labor force participation declining to 59.1% by 2030 (from 62.6% baseline), representing roughly 10 million fewer workers, with AI accounting for approximately half the decline.
By 2050 in the rapid scenario, top-10% wealth concentration reaches 80%, a level last seen in 1939, suggesting AI could dramatically widen wealth inequality.
A key tension: economists expect significant AI capabilities but economic indicators remaining near historical trends, citing multi-decade diffusion lags, uneven adoption, and demographic headwinds.

A retraining program could increase labor force participation by 1 percentage point (2.76 million workers) and boost GDP growth by 0.2 percentage points in rapid scenarios, though economists are skeptical of job guarantee programs (13.7% support vs. 57.1% public support).
methodology: Survey conducted October 2025 to February 2026, sampling 69 leading economists, 52 AI industry/policy experts, 38 superforecasters, and 401 general public members. Respondents provided probabilistic forecasts for multiple AI progress scenarios and their economic consequences across GDP, employment, labor force participation, and wealth distribution metrics at 2030 and 2050 horizons. Organized by FRI with institutional partners at the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, Yale, Stanford, and UPenn.
qualifiers: Expert forecasts of technology impact have a poor historical track record, and the wide disagreement between respondent groups underscores deep uncertainty. The scenarios (moderate, rapid) are stylized and may not capture the actual trajectory of AI development. Sample sizes are modest (69 economists, 52 AI experts), and selection of 'leading' respondents introduces potential bias. Forecasts at the 2050 horizon are especially uncertain. The survey captures beliefs, not evidence-based predictions, and respondent incentives may differ from those of prediction market participants.
